claims.text: κ is the ratio of short-range interactions between close-packed planes.
Compositional tuning of κ in FCC high-entropy alloys can promote multiple nanoscale stacking sequences.
κ-guided alloy design can simultaneously improve strength and ductility relative to extensively studied CoCrNi-based systems.
κ-guided alloy design can also improve Young's modulus and fracture resistance.
The initial CoCrNi-based systems have conventional stacking-fault energies and only limited populations of nanoscale twins or alternative stacking sequences.
A κ value near a critical degeneracy point for stacking sequences can be reached through systematic variation of elemental constituents.
Maintaining the FCC phase and suppressing undesirable precipitates are necessary conditions for the proposed improvement.
The effect should operate at room temperature and may extend to cryogenic temperatures.
Strain rates that allow sufficient time for dynamic microstructural evolution should favor the proposed effect.
Tuning κ will increase the density of stacking faults, nanotwins, and coexisting close-packed stacking sequences.
Multiple close-packed stacking sequences enhance work hardening and can contribute to both strength and ductility.
Near-degeneracy of stacking-fault energies lowers the activation barriers for forming twins and HCP-like fault regions.
Stress-driven microstructural reconfiguration balances dislocation mobility against obstacle formation.
The optimized alloys will improve yield strength, fracture strain, Young's modulus, and fracture toughness relative to conventional CoCrNi-based systems.
One or more mechanical metrics will improve by 5–20%.
Current CoCrNi-based alloys have good strength-ductility combinations whose behavior has been linked primarily to intrinsic stacking-fault energy.
Loss of the FCC phase, secondary-phase formation, excessive precipitation, or extreme strain rates may eliminate the proposed synergy.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis asserts simultaneous improvement of strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance, whereas the predicted outcome quantifies improvement for only one or more metrics.

The hypothesis requires simultaneous improvement across four properties, but the falsification rule requires significant improvement in only at least two properties, so an outcome that fails the central simultaneous-improvement claim could nevertheless pass the stated test.

The predicted range begins at 5%, while the falsification rule ambiguously treats improvements below approximately 5–10% as failure; outcomes between 5% and 10% could therefore be both predicted and potentially classified as falsifying.
